 as a tale of stubbornness and imagination, of men who dared to stand against the wind and the sea and who, in the course of a few centuries, turned the lonely, jagged rocks that rose from the water into beacons of safety for the countless vessels that plied the trade routes of Europe and the New World. In the earliest days, when the first wooden towers rose on the coasts of Ireland, Scotland, and the rugged shorelines of England, the idea of a permanent light was still a modest one. A simple fire, tended by a keeper who lived in a small stone cottage, was set upon a wooden framework, the flames licking the night sky and sending up a thin column of smoke that could be seen for a few miles. These early structures, often nothing more than a raised platform of timber, were vulnerable to the relentless battering of Atlantic storms, to the rot that set in when the sea spray soaked the wood, and to the ever-present threat of fire. Yet even in these primitive beginnings, the notion that a fixed point of light could guide a ship through treacherous waters took root, and the need for something more durable began to grow as commerce expanded and the number of ships crossing the Atlantic multiplied.

The transition from wood to stone was a natural one, for stone promised a resilience that timber could never match. In the early thirteenth century, the first stone towers began to appear along the coast of Cornwall and the western seaboard of England, their thick walls of locally quarried granite and limestone rising against the wind like silent guardians. These early stone lighthouses were built by masons who knew how to shape the stone so that it could bear the weight of the tower and resist the constant onslaught of salt and spray. The keepers who tended these beacons lived in small chambers within the walls, their lives intertwined with the rhythm of the sea. The light itself remained a simple fire, fed by wood or coal, and the illumination was modest, but the stone tower offered a permanence that the wooden structures could not. The idea that a lighthouse could be a permanent fixture on the coast, a fixed point of safety, began to take hold, and with it came the ambition to place these towers in ever more dangerous places.

One of the most famous early attempts to build a lighthouse on a dangerous rock was the Eddystone, a small outcrop off the coast of Plymouth, which had claimed many ships and lives. The first Eddystone lighthouse, erected in the early seventeenth
